entries.title: Colour Theory Basics
entries.subject: Design
entries.outline:
## Colour Theory Basics

Colour theory is the set of guidelines for mixing colours and combining them so a composition feels intentional rather than accidental.

The colour wheel organises hue; value and saturation do most of the perceptual work; a few standard schemes cover most needs.

## Why it matters
It is the difference between a design that looks intentional and one that looks accidental, and it takes only a few rules.

## The core ideas
- Hue is the colour name, value is lightness, saturation is intensity
- Complementary colours sit opposite and create maximum contrast
- Analogous colours sit adjacent and feel harmonious
- Warm colours advance, cool colours recede

## How it works, step by step
1. Choose a dominant hue that sets the mood
2. Pick a scheme: complementary, analogous, triadic or monochromatic
3. Set a value structure first — where is the lightest and darkest point
4. Use saturation sparingly; let one area be the most vivid
5. Test in greyscale to check the composition still reads

## A worked example
A poster uses a deep blue background (cool, recedes) with a single high-saturation orange headline (its complement). The eye jumps straight to the text because it is the only warm, vivid element against a calm field.

## Where people go wrong
- Using many fully saturated colours at once, so nothing stands out
- Ignoring value — a design can fail in greyscale even with 'nice' colours
- Treating the colour wheel as rules rather than starting points

## The takeaway
Pick one dominant hue, control value and saturation, and let a single accent do the shouting.

entries.title: Supply and Demand
entries.subject: Economics
entries.outline:
## Supply and Demand

Supply and demand is the model of how prices and quantities are set in a competitive market by the interaction of buyers and sellers.

The market clears where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer; shifts in either curve move that equilibrium.

## Why it matters
It is the most useful model in economics: it explains prices, shortages, surpluses and why price controls often backfire.

## The core ideas
- Demand slopes down: lower price, more wanted
- Supply slopes up: higher price, more produced
- Equilibrium is the price where the two quantities match
- A change in price moves along a curve; a change in anything else shifts the whole curve

## How it works, step by step
1. Draw demand and supply on price–quantity axes
2. Find the intersection: the equilibrium price and quantity
3. Identify the shock — a change in income, input costs, tastes or expectations
4. Shift the relevant curve and read off the new equilibrium
5. State the direction of change in both price and quantity

## A worked example
A frost destroys half the coffee crop. Supply shifts left. At the old price there is now a shortage, so price rises and quantity falls until buyers and remaining sellers agree again — a higher price, a smaller quantity.

## Where people go wrong
- Confusing a shift of a curve with a movement along it
- Shifting demand when the real cause was a price change
- Assuming price controls make shortages or surpluses disappear

## The takeaway
Price settles where quantity demanded meets quantity supplied; outside shocks shift a curve and move that point.

entries.title: Compound Interest
entries.subject: Finance
entries.outline:
## Compound Interest

Compound interest is interest earned on both the original principal and the interest already accumulated, so a balance grows faster over time.

Future value = P·(1 + r/n)^(n·t): compounding more often and waiting longer both increase the result, but time matters most.

## Why it matters
It is why starting to save at 25 beats saving twice as much at 45, and why credit-card debt grows so fast.

## The core ideas
- Simple interest grows linearly; compound interest grows exponentially
- The rule of 72: divide 72 by the percent rate to estimate the doubling time
- More frequent compounding helps, with diminishing returns toward continuous compounding
- Inflation compounds too, so compare real (after-inflation) returns

## How it works, step by step
1. Identify the principal, the annual rate, the compounding frequency and the time
2. Convert the rate per period: r/n
3. Raise (1 + r/n) to the number of periods n·t
4. Multiply by the principal to get the future value
5. Subtract the principal to isolate the interest earned

## A worked example
£1,000 at 6% compounded annually becomes £1,000·(1.06)^30 ≈ £5,743 after 30 years. At simple interest it would be only £1,000 + 30·£60 = £2,800. The extra £2,943 is interest on interest.

## Where people go wrong
- Using the annual rate without dividing by the number of periods
- Underestimating how much the last decade contributes
- Ignoring fees and inflation, which compound against you

## The takeaway
Compounding pays interest on your interest, so starting early beats saving more later.

entries.title: The Cold War
entries.subject: History
entries.outline:
## The Cold War

The Cold War was the decades-long geopolitical rivalry (roughly 1947–1991) between the United States and the Soviet Union, fought through proxy wars, alliances, propaganda and an arms race rather than direct combat.

Two superpowers with opposed ideologies and nuclear arsenals competed for global influence while avoiding direct war under the logic of mutual deterrence.

## Why it matters
It shaped nearly every border, alliance and proxy conflict of the late twentieth century, and its nuclear standoff still exists.

## The core ideas
- Ideological split: liberal capitalism versus state socialism
- Nuclear weapons made direct war unthinkable — 'mutually assured destruction'
- Competition ran through proxies: Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Latin America
- Alliances hardened into NATO and the Warsaw Pact

## How it works, step by step
1. Post-war Europe divides; the Iron Curtain falls across the continent
2. The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan commit the US to containment
3. Crises peak — the Berlin blockade, Cuba 1962 — then pull back from the brink
4. Détente in the 1970s eases tensions with arms-control treaties
5. Soviet economic stagnation and reform under Gorbachev end with the USSR's collapse in 1991

## A worked example
In October 1962 US reconnaissance found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Thirteen days of brinkmanship ended with a secret deal: the USSR withdrew the missiles, the US pledged not to invade Cuba and quietly removed missiles from Turkey.

## Where people go wrong
- Picturing it as constant crisis — long stretches were stable stalemate
- Treating every regional conflict as purely a superpower puppet show
- Assuming the outcome was inevitable

## The takeaway
Two nuclear superpowers competed everywhere except the battlefield, until one side's system gave out.

entries.title: The Industrial Revolution
entries.subject: History
entries.outline:
## The Industrial Revolution

The Industrial Revolution was the shift, beginning in Britain around 1760, from hand production and agriculture to machine manufacturing, factories and steam power.

New energy sources, mechanised textile production and the factory system multiplied output and reshaped where and how people lived.

## Why it matters
It created the modern world: cities, factories, wage labour, mass production and the fossil-fuel economy we still live with.

## The core ideas
- Steam power freed factories from rivers and multiplied available energy
- Textiles led: the spinning jenny, water frame and power loom
- Urban populations exploded as workers moved to factory towns
- Railways collapsed travel times and knit markets together

## How it works, step by step
1. Agricultural improvements raised food output and freed labour
2. Coal and iron industries expanded to feed machinery and rails
3. Textile inventions moved spinning and weaving into powered mills
4. The factory system concentrated workers, capital and machines under one roof
5. Railways and steamships spread the model across Europe and North America

## A worked example
In 1750 a handloom weaver in a cottage might produce a few metres of cloth a day. By 1850 a single Lancashire mill worker tending powered looms produced many times that — at a fraction of the cost, but on the mill's schedule, not their own.

## Where people go wrong
- Treating it as a single sudden event rather than a decades-long process
- Ignoring the social costs: child labour, pollution, unsafe factories
- Assuming every country industrialised the same way or at the same time

## The takeaway
Machines, coal and the factory turned scarce, slow handcraft into cheap mass production — and moved life into the city.

entries.title: Building a Clear Paragraph
entries.subject: Writing
entries.outline:
## Building a Clear Paragraph

A clear paragraph develops one idea, stated up front and supported by evidence, so a reader can follow the argument without rereading.

Topic sentence, then support, then a link back or forward: unity and coherence do the work.

## Why it matters
Clear paragraphs are the unit of every essay, report and email, and fixing them is the fastest way to write more persuasively.

## The core ideas
- One paragraph carries one controlling idea
- The topic sentence names that idea, usually first
- Evidence and explanation alternate — claim, proof, reasoning
- Transitions signal how each sentence relates to the last

## How it works, step by step
1. State the single point the paragraph will make
2. Give the strongest piece of evidence for it
3. Explain how that evidence supports the point
4. Add a second example or address an objection
5. Close by linking to the thesis or the next paragraph

## A worked example
Weak: five loosely related sentences about a novel's setting, mood and characters. Strong: a topic sentence claiming the setting mirrors the protagonist's isolation, then two quoted details, each followed by a sentence explaining the effect.

## Where people go wrong
- Starting with background and burying the point in the middle
- Listing evidence without explaining what it shows
- Letting one paragraph drift across two or three ideas

## The takeaway
Say the point first, prove it, explain the proof, then connect — one idea per paragraph.

entries.title: Bayes' Theorem
entries.subject: Mathematics
entries.outline:
## Bayes' Theorem

Bayes' theorem updates the probability of a hypothesis in light of new evidence, combining a prior belief with the likelihood of what was observed.

P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E): the posterior is the prior times the likelihood, normalised.

## Why it matters
It is how you should update beliefs from evidence, and ignoring it is why people badly misjudge medical tests and rare-event risks.

## The core ideas
- The prior P(H) is your belief before seeing the evidence
- The likelihood P(E|H) is how expected the evidence is if H is true
- The base rate dominates when the evidence is weak or the condition is rare
- Rare conditions make even accurate tests produce many false positives

## How it works, step by step
1. Write down the prior probability of the hypothesis
2. Write the likelihood of the evidence under the hypothesis and under its negation
3. Compute the total probability of the evidence P(E)
4. Divide to get the posterior P(H|E)
5. Iterate: today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior

## A worked example
A disease affects 1 in 1000 people. A test is 99% accurate both ways. You test positive. P(disease | positive) = (0.99 · 0.001) / (0.99 · 0.001 + 0.01 · 0.999) ≈ 0.09 — only about 9%, because healthy false positives vastly outnumber true cases.

## Where people go wrong
- Ignoring the base rate and reading test accuracy as the answer
- Swapping P(E|H) and P(H|E)
- Forgetting to include the false-positive path in P(E)

## The takeaway
Bayes' theorem rescales your prior by how well the hypothesis predicted the evidence.

entries.title: Derivatives and the Chain Rule
entries.subject: Mathematics
entries.outline:
## Derivatives and the Chain Rule

The derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function; the chain rule differentiates compositions of functions.

If y depends on u and u depends on x, then dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx — rates of change multiply along the chain.

## Why it matters
Rates of change appear everywhere, and the chain rule is the tool that makes almost every real-world derivative computable.

## The core ideas
- The derivative is the slope of the tangent line, the limit of the difference quotient
- Power, product and quotient rules cover most elementary combinations
- The chain rule handles 'a function inside a function'
- Differentiability implies continuity, but not the reverse

## How it works, step by step
1. Identify the outer function and the inner function
2. Differentiate the outer function, leaving the inner one untouched
3. Multiply by the derivative of the inner function
4. Simplify, and substitute back if you introduced a helper variable
5. Check units or limiting behaviour for a sanity test

## A worked example
Differentiate y = (3x² + 1)⁵. Outer: u⁵ → 5u⁴. Inner: 3x² + 1 → 6x. So dy/dx = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ · 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.

## Where people go wrong
- Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inside
- Applying the power rule to the whole expression as if the inside were just x
- Confusing the chain rule with the product rule

## The takeaway
To differentiate a composition, differentiate the outside, keep the inside, then multiply by the inside's derivative.

entries.title: DNA Replication
entries.subject: Biology
entries.outline:
## DNA Replication

DNA replication is the semi-conservative process that copies a cell's genome before division, so each daughter cell receives an identical set of instructions.

Each strand of the double helix serves as a template for a new complementary strand, producing two helices that each keep one old strand.

## Why it matters
Every time a cell divides it must copy three billion base pairs almost perfectly; the same machinery is the target of many cancer drugs and antibiotics.

## The core ideas
- Replication is semi-conservative — proven by the Meselson–Stahl experiment
- It starts at defined origins and proceeds in both directions
- DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides 5' to 3', so one strand is made continuously and one in fragments
- Proofreading by polymerase keeps the error rate near 1 in 10^9 bases

## How it works, step by step
1. Helicase unwinds the double helix at the origin, forming a replication fork
2. Single-strand binding proteins hold the strands apart; topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead
3. Primase lays down a short RNA primer
4. DNA polymerase III extends the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand as Okazaki fragments
5. DNA polymerase I replaces primers with DNA; ligase seals the nicks

## A worked example
On the lagging strand, primase must repeatedly re-prime as the fork opens. Each Okazaki fragment is roughly 100–200 bases in eukaryotes, later stitched together by ligase into one continuous strand.

## Where people go wrong
- Saying both strands are synthesised continuously
- Forgetting that primers are RNA, not DNA
- Confusing helicase (unwinds) with polymerase (builds)

## The takeaway
Replication unzips the helix and builds a matching partner for each strand, one continuously and one in pieces.

entries.title: Natural Selection
entries.subject: Biology
entries.outline:
## Natural Selection

Natural selection is the process by which heritable traits that improve survival and reproduction become more common in a population over generations.

Given variation, heredity and differential reproductive success, allele frequencies shift toward traits that fit the current environment.

## Why it matters
It explains the fit between living things and their environment without appealing to design, and it is why antibiotic and pesticide resistance evolve.

## The core ideas
- Individuals vary, and some of that variation is heritable
- More offspring are produced than the environment can support
- Traits that raise reproductive success spread; the process has no goal or foresight
- Selection acts on phenotypes but changes are recorded in allele frequencies

## How it works, step by step
1. A population shows heritable variation in a trait
2. The environment imposes a challenge — a predator, a drought, a new food source
3. Individuals with favourable variants survive and reproduce at higher rates
4. Their alleles are over-represented in the next generation
5. Over many generations the population's trait distribution shifts

## A worked example
On the Galápagos, a dry year leaves only large, hard seeds. Finches with deeper beaks crack them and survive; the next generation's average beak depth measurably increases — then partly reverses in a wet year.

## Where people go wrong
- Thinking individuals evolve — populations do
- Assuming selection produces perfect or 'advanced' organisms
- Confusing natural selection (a mechanism) with evolution (the outcome)

## The takeaway
Natural selection is heredity plus variation plus differential survival, compounding over generations.

entries.title: Photosynthesis
entries.subject: Biology
entries.outline:
## Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored as glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

The overall reaction takes carbon dioxide and water and, using light captured by chlorophyll, builds glucose and oxygen.

## Why it matters
Almost every food chain on Earth starts here, and photosynthesis is what keeps atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide in balance.

## The core ideas
- Light-dependent reactions run in the thylakoid membranes and produce ATP and NADPH
- The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma and fixes CO2 into sugar using that ATP and NADPH
- Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly and reflects green
- Only about 1–2% of incoming solar energy is captured as chemical energy

## How it works, step by step
1. Light strikes photosystem II and excites electrons, splitting water and releasing O2
2. Electrons pass down an electron transport chain, pumping protons to drive ATP synthase
3. Photosystem I re-energises the electrons to reduce NADP+ to NADPH
4. In the Calvin cycle, RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP; ATP and NADPH reduce it to G3P
5. Some G3P leaves to form glucose; the rest regenerates RuBP

## A worked example
A leaf in bright noon sun fixes CO2 quickly, but on a hot dry afternoon its stomata close to save water. CO2 inside the leaf falls, RuBisCO starts binding O2 instead (photorespiration) and the net sugar gain drops.

## Where people go wrong
- Confusing the light reactions (make ATP/NADPH) with the Calvin cycle (uses them)
- Thinking the Calvin cycle does not need light — it needs the products of the light reactions
- Assuming plants only respire at night; they respire continuously

## The takeaway
Photosynthesis turns light, water and CO2 into sugar and oxygen in two linked stages: energy capture, then carbon fixation.

entries.title: Acids, Bases and pH
entries.subject: Chemistry
entries.outline:
## Acids, Bases and pH

pH measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution on a logarithmic scale, capturing how acidic or basic that solution is.

Acids donate protons and bases accept them; pH = -log[H+], so each unit is a tenfold change in acidity.

## Why it matters
Blood, soil, oceans, medicines and food all depend on pH staying in a narrow range, and one unit is a tenfold change in acidity.

## The core ideas
- Pure water is neutral at pH 7 (25 °C) with [H+] = [OH-] = 1e-7 M
- Strong acids and bases dissociate fully; weak ones reach an equilibrium
- A buffer resists pH change by pairing a weak acid with its conjugate base
- pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C

## How it works, step by step
1. Identify whether the acid or base is strong or weak
2. For strong species, [H+] or [OH-] equals the concentration
3. For weak species, set up the Ka or Kb equilibrium expression
4. Solve for [H+], then take -log to get pH
5. For a buffer, apply the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

## A worked example
0.1 M HCl is a strong acid, so [H+] = 0.1 M and pH = 1. But 0.1 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8e-5) only partly dissociates: [H+] ≈ 1.3e-3 M, giving pH ≈ 2.9 — far less acidic at the same concentration.

## Where people go wrong
- Treating weak acids as if they fully dissociate
- Forgetting pH is logarithmic — pH 3 is 100× more acidic than pH 5
- Assuming a neutral solution is always pH 7 regardless of temperature

## The takeaway
pH is a log scale of proton concentration; strong species dissociate fully, weak ones sit at equilibrium.

entries.title: The Periodic Table
entries.subject: Chemistry
entries.outline:
## The Periodic Table

The periodic table arranges the elements by increasing atomic number so that elements with similar chemical behaviour fall into the same column.

Position predicts properties: reactivity, atomic radius, ionisation energy and typical charges all follow from where an element sits.

## Why it matters
It lets you predict how an unfamiliar element behaves from its position alone, which is the starting point for all of chemistry.

## The core ideas
- Rows are periods; columns are groups sharing a valence electron count
- Metals sit left and centre, non-metals top right, metalloids on the staircase
- Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group
- Ionisation energy and electronegativity increase across and up

## How it works, step by step
1. Read the atomic number to get the proton count and electron count of the neutral atom
2. Fill electron shells to find the valence electrons
3. Use the group to predict the common ion charge
4. Use period and group position to rank radius and ionisation energy
5. Predict bonding: metal + non-metal tends ionic, non-metal + non-metal tends covalent

## A worked example
Sodium (group 1) has one valence electron it loses easily, giving Na+. Chlorine (group 17) needs one, giving Cl-. They form the ionic solid NaCl, whereas two chlorine atoms share a pair to form covalent Cl2.

## Where people go wrong
- Reading group numbers off an old table with different conventions
- Assuming radius grows with atomic number in a straight line
- Forgetting that transition metals can show several oxidation states

## The takeaway
The table is a map: an element's row and column tell you how it will react.

entries.title: The Carbon Cycle
entries.subject: Environmental Science
entries.outline:
## The Carbon Cycle

The carbon cycle is the continuous movement of carbon between the atmosphere, oceans, living things, soils and rocks.

Carbon flows fast between air, life and surface ocean, and slowly into rock and fossil deposits; burning fossil fuels short-circuits the slow path into the fast one.

## Why it matters
Understanding it is what lets you see why burning fossil fuels changes the climate: it moves carbon from the slow cycle into the fast one.

## The core ideas
- Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the air; respiration and decay return it
- The ocean holds far more carbon than the atmosphere and exchanges it at the surface
- The slow cycle locks carbon in limestone and fossil fuels for millions of years
- Human emissions add roughly 10 billion tonnes of carbon a year to the fast cycle

## How it works, step by step
1. Plants and plankton fix atmospheric CO2 into organic carbon
2. Animals eat plants; respiration returns some carbon to the air
3. Dead matter decomposes, releasing CO2 or forming soil carbon
4. Over geological time, buried carbon becomes rock, coal, oil and gas
5. Weathering and volcanism slowly return that carbon to the surface

## A worked example
A carbon atom in a 2024 breath of CO2 might be absorbed by a tree next spring, released when a leaf decays two years later, dissolve into the ocean, and only after millennia settle into seafloor sediment.

## Where people go wrong
- Treating the atmosphere as the largest carbon store — the oceans and rocks hold much more
- Ignoring the timescale difference between the fast and slow cycles
- Assuming forests can absorb all human emissions

## The takeaway
Carbon shuttles quickly among air, life and ocean, and slowly into rock — and we are moving buried carbon back up fast.

entries.title: Electric Circuits
entries.subject: Physics
entries.outline:
## Electric Circuits

An electric circuit is a closed loop through which charge flows, driven by a voltage source and limited by the circuit's resistance.

Ohm's law (V = I·R) ties voltage, current and resistance; series and parallel arrangements combine components in predictable ways.

## Why it matters
Every device you use is a circuit, and understanding series and parallel behaviour is what lets you design, debug or stay safe around one.

## The core ideas
- Current is the same everywhere in a series loop; voltage splits across components
- Voltage is the same across parallel branches; current splits between them
- Resistances add in series; reciprocals add in parallel
- Power dissipated is P = V·I = I²·R

## How it works, step by step
1. Identify the source voltage and every resistor
2. Combine series and parallel resistors into one equivalent resistance
3. Use V = I·R to find the total current from the source
4. Work backwards to find the voltage across and current through each component
5. Check with Kirchhoff's laws: currents into a node sum to zero, voltages around a loop sum to zero

## A worked example
A 12 V battery drives two 6 Ω resistors in series. Total R = 12 Ω, so I = 1 A everywhere. Each resistor drops 6 V. Put the same two in parallel and R = 3 Ω, I_total = 4 A, with 2 A in each branch.

## Where people go wrong
- Assuming current is 'used up' as it goes around the loop
- Adding parallel resistances directly instead of reciprocals
- Mixing up which quantity stays constant in series vs parallel

## The takeaway
Voltage pushes, resistance limits, current flows; series shares current, parallel shares voltage.

entries.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
entries.subject: Physics
entries.outline:
## Newton's Laws of Motion

Newton's three laws relate the forces on an object to its motion, forming the foundation of classical mechanics.

An object's acceleration is set by the net force on it and its mass; forces always come in equal and opposite pairs.

## Why it matters
They predict the motion of everything from a thrown ball to a spacecraft, and every later mechanics course builds on them.

## The core ideas
- First law: with zero net force, velocity stays constant (inertia)
- Second law: F_net = m·a, a vector equation
- Third law: every force has an equal and opposite reaction on a different body
- Weight is a force (m·g); mass is the amount of matter

## How it works, step by step
1. Draw a free-body diagram showing every force on the object
2. Choose axes and resolve forces into components
3. Sum the forces along each axis to get the net force
4. Apply F_net = m·a along each axis
5. Solve for the unknown — acceleration, tension, friction or normal force

## A worked example
A 2 kg book sits on a table. Gravity pulls down with 19.6 N; the table pushes up with 19.6 N. Net force is zero, so by the first law the book stays at rest. Push it with 5 N against 3 N of friction and it accelerates at (5−3)/2 = 1 m/s².

## Where people go wrong
- Thinking a moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving
- Pairing the wrong forces as 'action–reaction' (they act on different bodies)
- Confusing mass and weight

## The takeaway
Net force equals mass times acceleration; no net force means no change in motion.

entries.title: Classical and Operant Conditioning
entries.subject: Psychology
entries.outline:
## Classical and Operant Conditioning

Conditioning is learning through association: classical conditioning links two stimuli, while operant conditioning links a behaviour to its consequence.

Classical conditioning is about what precedes a reflex; operant conditioning is about what follows a voluntary action.

## Why it matters
These two mechanisms explain phobias, habits, advertising and training from a handful of simple rules.

## The core ideas
- Classical: a neutral stimulus paired with a meaningful one comes to trigger the response
- Operant: reinforcement increases a behaviour, punishment decreases it
- Reinforcement and punishment can each be positive (add) or negative (remove)
- Intermittent reinforcement produces behaviour that is hard to extinguish

## How it works, step by step
1. Decide whether the behaviour is a reflex (classical) or a chosen action (operant)
2. For classical, name the unconditioned stimulus, response, and the neutral stimulus being paired
3. For operant, name the behaviour and its consequence
4. Classify the consequence: positive/negative, reinforcement/punishment
5. Predict the change in behaviour frequency over repeated trials

## A worked example
A dog hears a bell before every meal and starts salivating at the bell alone — classical. Later it learns that pressing a lever produces a treat and presses more often — operant, positive reinforcement.

## Where people go wrong
- Calling negative reinforcement a punishment — it removes something unpleasant to increase behaviour
- Assuming punishment teaches the right behaviour rather than just suppressing one
- Mixing up which type applies to reflexes versus choices

## The takeaway
Classical conditioning trains a trigger; operant conditioning trains a habit through its consequences.

entries.title: Big-O Notation
entries.subject: Computer Science
entries.outline:
## Big-O Notation

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input size grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.

It captures the dominant term of the cost function, so O(2n + 5) is just O(n) and O(3n² + n) is O(n²).

## Why it matters
It tells you whether a program will still work when the data gets 100 times bigger, which is the difference between a prototype and a product.

## The core ideas
- It is an upper bound on growth, not an exact running time
- Common classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)
- Constants and machine speed do not change the class
- Best, average and worst cases can differ (quicksort: O(n log n) vs O(n²))

## How it works, step by step
1. Count the operations as a function of input size n
2. Drop constant factors and additive constants
3. Keep only the fastest-growing term
4. Name the class and note whether it is best, average or worst case
5. Compare against alternatives at large n, not small n

## A worked example
A nested loop over an array of length n does about n·n = n² comparisons — O(n²). Adding a single pass afterward gives n² + n operations, still O(n²) because n² dominates as n grows.

## Where people go wrong
- Reporting O(n² + n) instead of O(n²)
- Assuming a lower Big-O always wins for small inputs
- Confusing time complexity with actual wall-clock time

## The takeaway
Big-O names the shape of the growth curve, not the exact cost.

entries.title: How HTTPS Works
entries.subject: Computer Science
entries.outline:
## How HTTPS Works

HTTPS is HTTP carried over a TLS connection, which authenticates the server and encrypts everything exchanged between browser and site.

A TLS handshake uses asymmetric cryptography to agree a shared secret, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the session.

## Why it matters
It is what makes online banking, logins and private messaging possible, and it tells you exactly what a padlock does and does not promise.

## The core ideas
- The certificate proves the server owns the domain, signed by a trusted CA
- Asymmetric keys set up the connection; symmetric keys carry the data
- Modern TLS uses ephemeral keys so past traffic stays safe if a key leaks (forward secrecy)
- The browser verifies the certificate chain up to a root it trusts

## How it works, step by step
1. The client sends a hello with supported cipher suites and a random value
2. The server replies with its certificate and its own random value
3. The client verifies the certificate chain and expiry
4. Both sides derive the same session keys via a key-exchange algorithm
5. All further HTTP messages are encrypted and integrity-protected with those keys

## A worked example
You open a bank site. The browser checks the certificate names match the domain and chains to a trusted root. A Diffie–Hellman exchange produces a shared key neither an eavesdropper nor a future attacker with the server's private key can recover.

## Where people go wrong
- Thinking HTTPS hides which site you visited (the domain is often still visible)
- Believing a padlock means the site is trustworthy, only that the channel is encrypted
- Confusing hashing with encryption

## The takeaway
HTTPS authenticates the server with a certificate, then encrypts the session with a freshly negotiated shared key.
